title: How can a building survive through change?
essentialQuestion: How can a building survive through change?
learningGoal: Tell a building's materials apart from the knowledge used to look after it, explain how Djenné's earthen mosque is cared for, and describe why conserving a living place involves the people who use it.

evidence.question: Djenné, Mali, West Africa; an Islamic urban setting, regional earthen-building knowledge and continuing community life. Look at the wider view first, then at the closer one.

sections.heading: A building people keep working on
sections.text:
A building can last for generations because people keep working on it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different kinds of care. Some materials need regular renewal, so keeping a place does not always mean leaving every surface untouched. Conservation is care that helps valued heritage last. It means understanding what matters about a building, and how its material, use and meaning can continue.

The Great Mosque of Djenné stands in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO names the Old Towns of Djenné as an important example of earthen architecture: building with materials made from earth. The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906–1907. That date matters. The building we see is connected with a longer religious and urban history. But its present structure should not simply be described as unchanged since medieval times.
sections.simpler:
A building can last a long time because people keep working on it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different care. Some materials must be renewed often. So keeping a place does not always mean leaving it untouched. Conservation is care that helps a valued place last. It means knowing what matters about a building, and how to keep it going.

The Great Mosque of Djenné is in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO says the old towns of Djenné are a key example of earthen architecture. That means buildings made with earth. The mosque we see now was rebuilt in 1906 and 1907. The town's history is much older. But we should not say this building has stayed the same for hundreds of years.

sections.heading: Trade, learning and skilled building
sections.text:
The town's wider setting explains why this mosque mattered. Djenné grew as a market centre connected with the trans-Saharan gold trade, the trade in gold across the Sahara Desert. It became important for the spread of Islam in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Waterways also linked the town with other trading places. Trade, religious learning and local building knowledge belonged to the same urban history. Islamic identity did not require copying one form of building used everywhere. People used regional materials and skills to make a place of worship suited to their setting.

Earth is a skilled building material here. UNESCO's Urban Heritage Atlas describes sun-baked earth bricks coated with mud plaster. The wooden pieces that stick out from the walls, and the shaped surfaces, give the mosque a distinctive look. The photographs in this lesson show parts of the outside in 2005. They record what was visible then; they do not show the building's condition today.
sections.simpler:
Djenné grew as a market town. It was linked to a trade in gold across the Sahara Desert. In the 1400s and 1500s, it became important in the spread of Islam. Waterways, such as rivers, linked it to other trading towns. Trade, religious learning and building skills grew up together there. Muslims did not have to copy one style of building. People here used local materials and skills. They made a mosque that suits its place.

Earth is a skilled building material here. The bricks are made of earth and dried in the sun. Builders cover them with mud plaster. Wooden pieces stick out from the walls. The photos in this lesson were taken in 2005. They show how the mosque looked then, not how it looks today.

sections.heading: Care, knowledge and the people of Djenné
sections.text:
Looking after earthen buildings depends on knowledge and cooperation. The atlas describes Djenné's masons, the skilled builders, and how building skills are passed on. It also names the yearly plastering of the mosque as a practice that connects two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the physical building. Intangible heritage is the knowledge, organisation and shared practices around it. People take part in the life of the place through work as well as worship.

Regular care does not prevent every problem. A UNESCO report from December 2009 describes extra restoration and strengthening work involving traditional masons. Restoration is work to recover or make clearer an earlier form or condition. This dated report shows that yearly surface care and specialist repairs to the structure are different kinds of work. It should not be read as a current report of an emergency still going on.

Djenné is also a town where people live, trade and learn, and want comfortable homes and public services. Conservation needs to consider those lives. Treating a place only as attractive scenery can leave out the people whose knowledge keeps it going. A careful account asks which features carry historical and cultural meaning, and how they are looked after. It also asks how decisions involve the communities who use them.
sections.simpler:
Caring for earth buildings takes knowledge and teamwork. Djenné's masons are skilled builders. They pass their skills on to others. Every year, people put new plaster on the mosque. This links two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the building itself. Intangible heritage is the knowledge and shared ways of doing things. People help the mosque through work as well as worship.

Yearly care cannot stop every problem. In December 2009, UNESCO reported extra repair work by traditional masons. Restoration is work to bring back an earlier form or condition. So yearly plastering and big repairs are different jobs. That report is from 2009. It does not describe a problem today.

People also live, trade and learn in Djenné. They want good homes and services. Conservation must think about their lives too. A place is not just a pretty view. The people who keep it going matter. Good choices include the people who use the place.

glossary.definition: Care that helps a valued building, object or place last.
glossary.example: The conservation of the mosque includes new plaster every year.

glossary.definition: Buildings made with materials that come from the earth, such as mud.
glossary.example: Djenné is famous for its earthen architecture.

glossary.definition: Places or things from the past that you can see and touch.
glossary.example: The mosque's walls are tangible heritage.

glossary.definition: Knowledge, skills and shared ways of doing things that people pass on.
glossary.example: The masons' skills are intangible heritage.

glossary.definition: Work to bring back an earlier form or condition.
glossary.example: The 2009 restoration made parts of the building stronger.

write.prompt: Explain why caring for the mosque needs both materials and people's knowledge. Use one detail of each from the reading.
write.example: The mosque is made of earth bricks dried in the sun and covered with mud plaster. This material needs care again and again, so people plaster the mosque every year. People's knowledge matters because Djenné's masons know how to do this work and pass their skills on. So the building lasts because of both its earth and the people who look after it.

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, explain the difference between the yearly plastering and the extra repair work in the 2009 report.
speak.independentTask: Say or type a short explanation of the difference between yearly care and the extra repair work described in 2009.

sensitiveNotes: The Great Mosque is a working place of worship. Teach Islam and the mosque respectfully, as part of the town's living history. No learner is asked to share their religion or to perform a practice.
educatorNotes: Misconception to watch for: authentic heritage must never change, or building with earth shows a lack of skill. Both hide the documented techniques and the continuing social life of Djenné.

Answer points for Write: earth bricks and mud plaster need suitable, regular care; masons and community practices keep the knowledge and the organised work going. Regular renewal can sustain a heritage place, while particular restoration decisions still need evidence. Simple English is fine.

Neither photograph shows the yearly replastering; don't imply that it does. Both date from 2005 and do not show the building's condition today. The second photo's record dates it 19 March 2005, but the camera's date print in its corner does not obviously match; treat the date as the record's.

The UNESCO site page, the Urban Heritage Atlas and the 2009 report have different dates and purposes; don't present older management periods or assessments as current figures, or the 2009 work as a current emergency. The atlas's own images have mixed rights and are not the source of these CC BY photographs.

Don't merge the present town and mosque with the older archaeological site of Djenné-Djeno, or with the borders of a single medieval empire. The trade, Islam and waterway context comes from the UNESCO site record and the atlas.
